Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit.

We represent: defendant employer.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that temporal proximity alone, absent unusually suggestive timing, is insufficient to establish causation for a retaliation claim.

Cite at least six decisions of the Third Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

## ARGUMENT

### Temporal proximity alone, absent unusually suggestive timing, cannot establish the causal link required for a retaliation claim.

To establish a prima facie case of retaliation, a plaintiff must show that (1) she engaged in protected activity, (2) the employer took an adverse action against her, and (3) a causal connection links the two. *Moore v. City of Philadelphia*, 461 F.3d 331, 340-41 (3d Cir. 2006). Plaintiff's claim fails at the third element. Her only evidence of causation is the sequence of events, and sequence alone does not carry her burden.

**A. Timing supports an inference of causation only when it is unusually suggestive.**

This Court has repeatedly held that temporal proximity can support causation by itself only when the timing is "unusually suggestive of retaliatory motive." *Krouse v. Am. Sterilizer Co.*, 126 F.3d 494, 503 (3d Cir. 1997). Where it is not, the plaintiff must produce other evidence from which a jury could infer a retaliatory link. *Williams v. Phila. Hous. Auth. Police Dep't*, 380 F.3d 751, 760 (3d Cir. 2004); *Lauren W. ex rel. Jean W. v. DeFlaminis*, 480 F.3d 259, 267 (3d Cir. 2007). The Court has been equally clear about the limits of timing as proof. In *Kachmar v. SunGard Data Systems, Inc.*, 109 F.3d 173, 177 (3d Cir. 1997), it explained that the causation inquiry looks to the record as a whole, not merely to the order of events. And in *Thomas v. Town of Hammonton*, 351 F.3d 108, 114 (3d Cir. 2003), it held that timing that falls short of the unusually suggestive threshold does not by itself permit an inference of causation.

The Supreme Court has set the same standard. It has approved reliance on temporal proximity only where the events are "very close" in time. *Clark Cnty. Sch. Dist. v. Breeden*, 532 U.S. 268, 273-74 (2001) (per curiam).

**B. Gaps of weeks or months fall outside the unusually suggestive category.**

The Third Circuit has consistently declined to treat a gap of any significant length as sufficient on its own. In *LeBoon v. Lancaster Jewish Community Center Ass'n*, 503 F.3d 217, 232-33 (3d Cir. 2007), the Court held that a three-month interval between the protected activity and the adverse action, without more, was insufficient to create an inference of causation. The Court has also treated timing that is merely close, as opposed to immediate, as the starting point for further inquiry and not the end of it. *Williams*, 380 F.3d at 759-60; *Daniels v. Sch. Dist. of Phila.*, 776 F.3d 181, 196-97 (3d Cir. 2015).

Here, [__] days/weeks/months separated Plaintiff's protected activity from [adverse action]. That interval is not so short that it alone suggests retaliation. It is the kind of gap this Court has found insufficient without further evidence.

**C. Plaintiff offers no other evidence of causation.**

Where timing is not unusually suggestive, a plaintiff may still prevail by pointing to "timing plus other evidence," such as a pattern of antagonism or inconsistent explanations for the employer's conduct. *Farrell v. Planters Lifesavers Co.*, 206 F.3d 271, 279-81 (3d Cir. 2000); *see also Marra v. Phila. Hous. Auth.*, 497 F.3d 286, 302 (3d Cir. 2007) (considering the record as a whole, including intervening conduct and any pattern of antagonism). Plaintiff has no such evidence. The record shows no pattern of antagonism after the protected activity and no inconsistency in Defendant's explanation. It shows no comparator evidence and no statement by a decisionmaker linking the [adverse action] to Plaintiff's protected activity. Defendant's legitimate, non-retaliatory reason, [__], has been consistent throughout.

Without those additional facts, Plaintiff has only the observation that one event followed another. *Farrell* and *Krouse* do not permit that sequence, standing alone, to substitute for proof of causation. A contrary rule would convert every adverse action that follows protected activity into a triable retaliation claim and would shield employees from legitimate employment decisions.

### Conclusion

Because the timing here is not unusually suggestive and Plaintiff has identified no other evidence of a causal link, she has not established the third element of her prima facie case. The judgment should be affirmed.
